stories.title: EvilTokens: a phishing-as-a-service kit that steals Microsoft 365 tokens through device code phishing
stories.summary: EvilTokens is a phishing-as-a-service platform that appeared in February 2026 and abuses the OAuth device code flow. Microsoft says its campaigns compromised more than 12,000 inboxes in over 10,000 organizations. The victim is shown a real device code and sent to the genuine microsoft.com/devicelogin page, so the sign-in and MFA are done by the victim and the attacker receives the tokens without ever seeing a password. Stolen tokens were used to read and exfiltrate mail, create inbox rules and in some cases register a device to obtain a Primary Refresh Token. Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit coordinated a disruption of the infrastructure. On 17 November 2026 Huntress reported that a joint Microsoft Digital Crimes Unit and FBI effort led to the arrest of one alleged EvilTokens operator.

timeline.text: EvilTokens emerges as a phishing-as-a-service platform sold through Telegram. (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Microsoft tracks a related campaign that used automation platforms to start short-lived polling nodes running Node.js backend logic. (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Microsoft Threat Intelligence publishes its analysis and describes the coordinated disruption by the Digital Crimes Unit.

Huntress, in a sponsored article on BleepingComputer, says it found EvilTokens in early 2026 abusing the Railway platform-as-a-service as a token-harvesting and replay engine, and that a joint effort of Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit and the FBI later led to the arrest of one of its alleged operators (no further detail given).

stories.rootCause: The device code flow lets a third party start a sign-in that the victim completes on a legitimate Microsoft page. Where Conditional Access does not block the flow, the attacker's polling script receives valid tokens after the victim signs in with MFA.
attacker: Developer and operator of the kit is tracked as Storm-2992; sold on Telegram for $1,500 plus $500 per month.

Lures by email (invoices, RFPs, shared files, password-expiry notices) with URLs, PDF or HTML attachments, behind fake CAPTCHA pages and multi-stage redirects on Vercel, Cloudflare Workers and AWS Lambda.
A background script requests a live device code, shows it with Copy Code and Continue buttons and polls the actor's /state endpoint every three to five seconds for up to 15 minutes.

After sign-in: Microsoft Graph reconnaissance, AI-assisted search for financial and executive mailboxes, wire-transfer and invoice keywords, malicious inbox rules, and device registration to obtain a Primary Refresh Token within about 10 minutes.
Used the Railway platform-as-a-service as a token-harvesting and replay engine (Huntress, via BleepingComputer, 17 November 2026).
iocs: Hosting abused: .vercel.app, .workers.dev, AWS Lambda (named by Microsoft)
Microsoft lists no IP addresses or file hashes in this post

remediation.text: Block the device code flow with Conditional Access wherever possible; where Teams devices need it, scope the exception to the Teams device resource accounts and exclude the Device Registration Service resource.
Revoke refresh tokens with revokeSignInSessions for a suspected account and consider disabling it temporarily; access tokens can stay valid for up to an hour.
Require phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO, Authenticator with passkeys), enable sign-in risk policies and Continuous Access Evaluation, block legacy authentication.
Configure anti-phishing, Safe Links and ZAP, raise the Advanced Phishing Threshold to 2 or 3 and alert on suspicious inbox rule creation.
Revoke the user's refresh tokens, then remove devices and Windows Hello credentials the attacker registered.

Hunt for device code authentication, automated token refresh and successful sign-ins from unfamiliar cloud infrastructure; review new devices, authentication methods, mailbox access, forwarding rules and outbound phishing.
Keep monitoring for token replay or re-entry after the phishing domain disappears.

stories.title: Storm-3168 (JADEPUFFER): agentic destructive attack in Azure through compromised service principals
stories.summary: Microsoft investigated malicious Azure activity in one compromised tenant where two service principals were used: one for reconnaissance, the other for discovery, bulk deletion and credential collection. More than 150 destructive or credential-collection operations ran over 35 minutes, hitting storage accounts, a Key Vault, a Function App and an App Service plan; SQL deletions failed on an unsupported API version and some deletions were stopped by resource locks. Microsoft saw no ransom note and did not confirm data exfiltration. The actor is tracked as Storm-3168 and is associated with JADEPUFFER, which Sysdig reported in July 2026 as the first documented agentic ransomware operation.

timeline.text: Early June: the first service principal enumerates VMs, subscriptions and resources for about 15.5 hours; the second follows about 90 minutes later and later enumerates App Service configuration stores. (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Sysdig discovers JADEPUFFER (as reported by Microsoft). (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Microsoft Security Research publishes the analysis.

stories.rootCause: Initial access is unconfirmed. Microsoft found a client ID, secret and tenant ID posted in plaintext in a public GitHub issue by an employee and still visible in the edit history, but could not confirm that credential was used. The service principals held broad Azure RBAC roles (Contributor, Storage Account Contributor, SQL DB Contributor), which made the deletions possible.
attacker: Used existing Azure RBAC assignments of the two service principals; five unique tokens for the destructive principal, two active in the same 70-second window, assessed as automated.
User agent python-requests/2.34.2 and shared infrastructure for both principals.
Tried to delete Azure Site Recovery and Azure Backup protection locks (failed), then listed storage account keys 30+ times after the destruction.
iocs: 45.131.66[.]106 (App Service probing and malicious ARM requests)

remediation.text: Treat publicly exposed credentials as compromised even after the source is edited: rotate immediately and review historical use.
Apply least privilege to service principals through Azure RBAC and prefer mechanisms that reduce long-lived credentials.
Use resource locks and deletion protection, restrict access to backup and recovery resources and monitor attempts to change their protection.
Enable the Defender for Cloud plans for Resource Manager, Storage, Key Vault, App Service and Databases.

stories.title: Beyond source code: a self-service password reset on one account led to Azure DevOps pipelines and Kubernetes credentials
stories.summary: Microsoft's Detection and Response Team described an intrusion that began with a single user account taken over through self-service password reset (SSPR). The attacker registered their own authentication methods, then used legitimate admin tools and scripts to enumerate Azure DevOps repositories, projects and pipelines. A malicious pipeline harvested Kubernetes credentials (kubeconfig files); pipeline scripts were then changed to install the Atera remote management agent and the Chisel tunnelling tool. The page attributes the activity to Storm-3068 and gives no attack dates and no IOC values. The case shows how an identity weakness spreads when development platforms, pipelines and cloud infrastructure are tightly connected.

timeline.text: Microsoft publishes the incident-response write-up; the page gives no dates for the intrusion itself.

stories.rootCause: Initial access was abuse of self-service password reset on a user account, followed by registration of attacker-controlled authentication methods. The impact grew because the account's permissions reached Azure DevOps pipelines authorised for more than 50 resources. The page does not state a formal root cause.
attacker: Took over a user account through self-service password reset and registered their own authentication methods.
Enumerated Azure DevOps repositories, projects, pipelines and deployment environments with legitimate tools and scripts.
Created a pipeline that deployed a kube agent and collected kubeconfig files at scale.
Modified pipeline scripts to install the Atera agent and download the Chisel tunnelling utility; Chisel opened a reverse tunnel to an external IP address (value not published).
Committed seven stolen kubeconfig files to a repository.

remediation.text: Monitor password reset activity for unusual patterns, such as repeated attempts or activity across multiple users.
Limit privileged accounts' exposure to self-service password reset and require phishing-resistant MFA.
Require approvals for code changes, enforce branch protection and restrict direct commits to critical branches.
Control who can create, modify or run build and deployment pipelines; apply least privilege across identities, development platforms and cloud resources.
Review recently registered authentication methods on accounts that completed a password reset, and review Azure DevOps audit logs for new or changed pipelines.

stories.title: Sideloaded AppX package abuses Microsoft-signed web hosts to capture OAuth tokens (Huntress research)
stories.summary: Huntress researcher Andrew Schwartz showed that a sideloaded AppX package can use Microsoft-signed AppX web hosts such as WWAHost.exe to show a genuine Microsoft sign-in, complete MFA and hand the authorization code to attacker JavaScript, which exchanges it for access and refresh tokens. It is post-compromise: it needs code execution in the user's session and Developer Mode or an enterprise sideloading policy. It was proven end to end on Windows 11 24H2 against a test tenant with MFA. Huntress names no threat actor and discloses no attacker infrastructure, so this is a technique, not an observed campaign. The Entra sign-in looks like a normal Office sign-in with no risk flags.

timeline.text: Huntress publishes the research; the page gives no date for the testing itself.

stories.rootCause: A design issue in the shared WinRT activation layer: a sideloaded package with WindowsRuntimeAccess="all" in ContentUriRules gives remote JavaScript the WinRT surface, with no caller validation, and the legacy WebAuthenticationBroker is reachable from inside the host. Developer Mode or the AllowAllTrustedApps policy is the gating condition.
attacker: Registers a package with Add-AppxPackage -Register as a standard user; the manifest points ContentUriRules at an attacker server.
Calls WebAuthenticationBroker.authenticateAsync() with Microsoft Office's first-party client ID and the urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob redirect URI.
The user sees a real Microsoft login with no address bar and completes MFA.
Receives the authorization code through the broker callback, exchanges it and exfiltrates the access and refresh tokens.
iocs: User agent MSAppHost/3.0 (Edge/18) reaching non-Microsoft destinations (broker leg: MSAuthHost/1.0)
Add-AppxPackage -Register from paths outside C:\Program Files\WindowsApps

remediation.text: Deploy the Sigma proxy rule on user agent MSAppHost/3.0 with a Microsoft domain allow-list tuned to your environment.
Audit Developer Mode across the fleet and disable 'Allow all trusted apps to install' by GPO.
Require compliant or managed devices for token issuance with Conditional Access and pair with Token Protection where available.
Shorten refresh-token lifetimes and enable Continuous Access Evaluation.

stories.title: Storm-0940 and the ARTEX AI framework: Microsoft ties the ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromise to a China-aligned actor
stories.summary: On 21 October Microsoft Threat Intelligence published its analysis of a large, AI-automated campaign by Storm-0940, which it describes as a China-state aligned actor active since 2021, using the open-source ARTEX penetration-testing framework. Microsoft says it assesses that Storm-0940 was responsible for the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise of the multi-tenant Cloud Backup application, and that the actor reached privileged cloud access in some cases less than three hours after first targeting. After taking control of ConnectWise application identities, the actor signed in to more than 2,250 downstream tenants through applications those customers had already trusted, and in some tenants moved on to Graph reconnaissance, credential additions to applications and privileged role changes, including one application that gave itself Global Administrator. Microsoft states this was not caused by a vulnerability in or compromise of Microsoft systems, and that a sign-in does not by itself prove data was accessed. The page does not say how the ConnectWise identities were first compromised. On 6 November Microsoft reported a second, unrelated actor (Storm-3358) using the same ARTEX framework against the financial sector, so ARTEX tooling alone does not identify Storm-0940.

timeline.text: Password-spray campaign starts from 144.172.64[.]99 against 327 accounts in eight organizations (10-14 Oct); about 151,000 failed logons, peak 2,900 failures per minute on 11 Oct.
Public reports of the ConnectWise compromise appear, citing IOCs in the same network range.
ConnectWise publishes an initial advisory, later expanded; one of its IPs matches 144.172.64[.]99.
Microsoft publishes the attribution and the hunting and detection guidance.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence reports that a different actor, the financially motivated Cambodia-based cluster Storm-3358, has used ARTEX against financial-sector organizations since October 2026 (indicators first seen 19 October to 4 November). Microsoft does not link Storm-3358 to Storm-0940 or to the ConnectWise compromise; it cites the 21 October post only as background on ARTEX.

stories.rootCause: Microsoft names no software vulnerability. The contributing factors it lists are compromised multi-tenant application identities holding high privileges, the trust and consent customers had already granted to those applications, password spraying against Microsoft 365 accounts, and machine-speed automation. It does not describe how the ConnectWise identities were initially compromised.
attacker: Used ARTEX, a multi-agent LLM framework that can run autonomous tests from reconnaissance to data exfiltration, to speed up targeting.
Ran a cross-tenant password spray against Microsoft 365 and Exchange Online (10-14 Oct).
Took control of identities of several ConnectWise cloud applications and used them to authenticate to customer tenants without interactive user sign-in (about 2,900 attempts per minute).

In some tenants: Graph and directory reconnaissance, application credential changes for persistence, changes to identities, groups and privileged roles; one application self-assigned Global Administrator (T1098.003).
Microsoft notes that backdoor credentials added to applications can survive remediation of the compromised application.
iocs: IP 144.172.64[.]99 (password spray; matches a ConnectWise advisory IP)
User agents Python-urllib/3.12, python-requests/2.31.0, python-requests/2.34.2, curl/7.88.1, azure-toolkit/1.0
ConnectWise application IDs 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae (Cloud Backup), 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640 (MS Teams), 0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827 (MS Graph)

remediation.text: Keep the affected ConnectWise application connections disabled until ConnectWise gives formal restoration instructions; do not delete the enterprise applications first, preserve configuration and evidence.
Inventory the application IDs above and record the local service principal object IDs in each tenant; search by application ID, not display name.

Preserve Entra sign-in and audit logs, Purview Audit records and Graph telemetry; review service-principal sign-ins from at least 15 Oct, extended to 1 Oct, successes and failures separately and not only the published IPs.

Review Entra audit records for credential additions, new apps, service principals or owners, app-role assignments, consent grants, privileged role assignments and changes to authentication methods or Conditional Access; review mailbox forwarding, inbox and transport rules and delegate permissions.
After preserving evidence, have an authorized responder remove confirmed unauthorized credentials, grants, owners, assignments and identities, revoke unneeded permissions and rotate credentials.
Apply least privilege to multi-tenant application permissions and consent grants; alert on credential additions, privileged role assignment and anomalous app-only activity.
An empty hunting result is not proof of no access: Microsoft says so explicitly, so check the audit trail as well.

Do not attribute ARTEX-style activity (bursts of varied requests, rapid retries, Nmap/curl/headless Chromium traffic) to Storm-0940 by tooling alone; Microsoft now reports Storm-3358 using ARTEX too. Rely on Entra ID Protection "Verified threat actor IP" detections and sign-in-risk Conditional Access as Microsoft recommends.

stories.title: PHP2Shell: two critical PHP remote code execution flaws (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
stories.summary: On 21 October 2026 the PHP project shipped emergency fixes for two critical flaws nicknamed PHP2Shell: CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state), both rated CVSS 4.0 9.2 by the sources. Every PHP installation serving web requests is affected, including PHP-FPM, mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. A working exploit exists that needs a single unauthenticated request, and Amazon recorded an exploitation attempt on 17 October, four days before disclosure. Sources disagree on in-the-wild exploitation after disclosure, so treat it as exploited. Palo Alto Networks says all PAN-OS and Panorama versions are affected with no fix yet. This is not a Microsoft product flaw; it matters to the SOC for web servers, App Service/IIS-PHP hosts and appliances in the estate.

timeline.text: Amazon MadPot honeypot records a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt.
PHP releases fixes in 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, 8.5.12 and source backports for 7.4, 8.0, 8.1; details leaked before the planned embargo.
Searchlight Cyber releases an open-source scanner; Palo Alto Networks confirms all PAN-OS and Panorama versions affected, no fix yet.

stories.rootCause: Memory-safety flaws in the PHP engine: out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while request data is only partly initialised (CVE-2026-109618), and request-owned state can outlive freed memory (CVE-2026-109619).
attacker: Unauthenticated remote code execution with a single request (per Help Net Security).
A pre-disclosure attempt from an IP tied to a commercial anonymisation service was seen by Amazon; how the exploit details were obtained is unknown.

remediation.text: Update PHP to 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 or 8.5.12, or install the distribution/LTS vendor backport; take offline any system that cannot be fixed immediately (UK NCSC).
Cloudflare WAF rules for known vectors are a partial control only, not a substitute for patching.
Inventory PHP hosts (web servers, App Service/containers, appliances) and PHP versions; scan with the Searchlight Cyber php2shell-scanner.
Hunt web-server and process telemetry on PHP hosts for unexpected child processes of php-fpm/apache/php-cgi and new files in web roots since 17 October.

stories.title: LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: credential theft through Python startup hooks
stories.summary: A malicious LiteLLM 1.107.0 was published to PyPI on 21 October 2026 and also shipped in official container images. It abused Python startup hooks (a .pth file and sitecustomize.py placed outside the litellm directory), so the payload ran when the Python interpreter started, even if LiteLLM was never imported. The collector gathers developer, cloud, CI/CD and AI-tool credentials, encrypts them and posts them to www[.]litellm[.]dev. Per the LiteLLM maintainers, stolen developer GitHub credentials were used to alter the release workflow; Microsoft did not determine how the attacker first got upstream access. Microsoft published detections on 22 October and its analysis on 23 October. Removing the package or a release tag is not sufficient recovery.

timeline.text: LiteLLM 1.107.0 published to PyPI and distributed through official container images.
Microsoft Defender detections and vulnerability management entry TVM-2026-0003 available.
Microsoft publishes its analysis, including hashes, detections and hunting queries.

stories.rootCause: Per LiteLLM maintainers (as relayed by Microsoft): stolen developer GitHub credentials were used to alter the release workflow so it pointed at the lookalike repository Berri-AI/litellm instead of BerriAI/litellm, and a credential from another developer account satisfied a production approval step. How the attacker first obtained upstream access is not determined.
attacker: Used Python startup hooks (MITRE T1546.018): cook.pth imports cook.py, which decodes an embedded collector (PRIVCOLLECT) and runs it in a daemon thread; sitecustomize.py adds a Unix path with a remote code loader.

Targeted developer and AI tool configs, git and package-manager credentials, dotenv and key files, AWS/Azure CLI/GCP/Kubernetes/Docker credentials, browser data, shell histories and LiteLLM proxy database fields.
Encrypted the data (AES-256-CBC, key wrapped with an embedded RSA-4096 key) and sent it by HTTP POST to /healthcheck; staging directories begin with .pc_e_.
Unix loader reads a GitHub-hosted domain.txt as a pointer to an attacker server and executes the /codepy response; when examined domain.txt was empty and no second stage was confirmed.
iocs: Further wheel and variant hashes are listed in the Microsoft article

remediation.text: Find every copy: installed environments, uv and pip caches, internal mirrors, lock files, build outputs and container images; compare against the published hashes and scope mutable container tags.
Investigate from a known-clean system; do not run python or pip inside a suspect environment, because site processing can trigger the payload.
Rebuild from verified artifacts and confirm cook.pth, cook.py and sitecustomize.py are gone from the library path; deleting only the litellm directory is insufficient.

Rotate credentials from a clean machine (model-provider keys, cloud and CI/CD secrets, source-control and registry tokens, SSH/GPG keys, AI coding-tool tokens, DATABASE_URL on proxy hosts) and revoke sessions, not only passwords.
Hash-pin lock files, verify provenance, use image digests and restrict outbound access from build and AI workloads.
Hunt in Defender XDR for connections to www.litellm.dev and the listed file hashes; review Entra sign-ins and cloud activity for identities whose secrets lived on affected hosts.

stories.title: Zimbra SNMP command injection (CVE-2026-73570): one crafted SMTP request gives a shell on internet-facing mail servers
stories.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes exploitation of CVE-2026-73570 in Zimbra Collaboration Suite servers that have the optional zimbra-snmp package installed and SNMP notifications enabled. A crafted SMTP request reaches SNMP notification processing, and when health monitoring fires, the swatchdog component passes the attacker's value into a snmptrap shell call, so commands run as the zimbra service account. Attackers deployed JSP webshells on every mailbox node, escalated to root through a writable log directory and a PAM hook, persisted with a fake zimlog.service unit, and pulled zimbraPreAuthKey, zimbraAuthTokenKey and two-factor secrets from LDAP. On one server mailbox backups were archived and AzCopy was run against an Azure Blob SAS URL; Microsoft does not confirm the transfer completed. Zimbra 10.1.20 (20 July 2026) fixes it.

timeline.text: Zimbra 10.1.20 released with the remediation.
Scanning and probing of the injection point begins (to 7 August), with out-of-band DNS, HTTP and ICMP callbacks and the User-Agent ZB73570.
Public disclosure of CVE-2026-73570.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence publishes the attack chain, detections, hunting queries and IOCs.

stories.rootCause: Insufficient sanitisation of input that reaches the snmptrap shell invocation built by swatchdog in the optional zimbra-snmp package; commands run with the privileges of the zimbra service account.
attacker: Probed with curl, wget, ping, nslookup and id callbacks (User-Agent ZB73570).
Wrote JSP webshells into Jetty and mailboxd paths on every mailbox node, copied with rsync over the zimbra SSH identity.
Escalated to root by symlinking zmmailboxd.out to /etc/pam.d/sudo, adding a pam_exec hook and a NOPASSWD sudoers entry for zimbra.
Persisted with a timestomped zimlog.service systemd unit, cron, OpenRC, shell startup files, SSH keys and local accounts.
Read service credentials with zmlocalconfig -s and LDAP secrets (zimbraPreAuthKey, zimbraAuthTokenKey, zimbraTwoFactorAuthSecret).
Staged /opt/zimbra/final.tar.gz and invoked AzCopy with an Azure Blob SAS URL.

remediation.text: Upgrade every Zimbra Collaboration Suite instance to 10.1.20 or later.
If patching must wait: uninstall zimbra-snmp, disable SNMP notifications and restrict SNMP and SMTP to trusted hosts.
Treat a reverse-shell alert on an internet-facing mail server as a priority incident.
Check Zimbra application and servlet work directories on every mailbox node for unexpected JSP files and recent permission changes; review systemd units, PAM files and sudoers.
Rotate every domain zimbraPreAuthKey, and treat zimbraAuthTokenKey and stored two-factor secrets as exposed on a compromised server.
Search beyond the 30 days of advanced hunting data in Sentinel or archived logs.
Onboard Linux mail servers to Defender for Endpoint and confine the service account with namespace, seccomp or AppArmor controls.
Search Azure Storage logs for writes from the mail servers' public IPs, and alert when AzCopy runs on a mail server.

stories.title: Star Blizzard RedFlick: one click from a phishing archive to the CosmicPulse backdoor via scheduled tasks
stories.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks RedFlick, a delivery technique used by the Russian state actor Star Blizzard from January to August 2026 against Ukrainian institutions, NGOs, think tanks, governments and financial institutions; Microsoft counts over 100 affected organizations, mostly in the US and UK. A first email without an attachment invites a reply; the follow-up carries a password-protected RAR or ZIP with the password shown as an image. Inside, an LNK disguised as a PDF runs SSH.exe with PermitLocalCommand or curl and PowerShell to fetch an MSI, which creates scheduled tasks that use control.exe to load the CosmicPulse downloader as a Control Panel applet. The post describes no OAuth, device-code or token abuse.

timeline.text: January campaign: VHDX with an LNK and BAT script that runs SSH.exe to fetch a remote MSI (activity observed from January).
From March, senders use accounts on compromised CPanel and WordPress sites instead of free mail services.
April: the MSI creates three scheduled tasks, including WebDAV loading through Control_RunDLL.
July: payload hidden in a downloaded PDF after the marker cAB, extracted by PowerShell.
August: steganography and a unique ZIP per target.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence publishes the analysis, detections, hunting queries and IOCs.

stories.rootCause: Social engineering: a reply-based phishing conversation followed by a password-protected archive that mail scanning cannot open, and a single user click on an LNK disguised as a PDF.
attacker: Sent tens to hundreds of lure emails per campaign impersonating Ukrainian authorities or conference invitations, some made to look internal.
Delivered password-protected RAR/ZIP archives with the password as an image.
Ran SSH.exe with PermitLocalCommand=yes and LocalCommand=cmd.exe, or conhost and curl, to fetch an MSI.

Created scheduled tasks (Internet Quality Test Connection, Network Configuration Manager, System Health Monitor) that use control.exe to load the CosmicPulse downloader (NOROBOT / BAITSWITCH) as a CPL.
Stored an encrypted AES key under HKCU\Software\Classes\.mollis and fetched a Python 3.8 bootstrapper and the CosmicPulse backdoor (YESROBOT).
iocs: secure-dns-hub[.]com (CosmicPulse DLL host, July to current)
Scheduled task names Internet Quality Test Connection, Network Configuration Manager, System Health Monitor

remediation.text: Use phishing-resistant authentication and Conditional Access policies.
Turn on Defender for Office 365 Safe Links, Safe Attachments and zero-hour auto purge.
Run EDR in block mode with cloud-delivered and real-time protection and network protection; enable ASR rules that block untrusted executables and obfuscated scripts.
Restrict outbound SSH from networks that do not need it.
Hunt for conhost.exe launching curl and ssh.exe with PermitLocalCommand=yes, and for the three scheduled task names; block the listed domains and IPs.
Alert on control.exe loading a CPL from a WebDAV UNC path or a user-writable folder, and quarantine password-protected archives from external senders for review.

stories.title: Token-replay spray against Microsoft 365: AiTM-stolen tokens replayed from 1337 Services hosting, 97 accounts at 79 organizations, attacker MFA and rogue Entra devices for persistence
stories.summary: Huntress (22 October 2026) describes a campaign observed from 14 July to 22 September 2026 in which tokens captured through adversary-in-the-middle phishing were replayed at scale from attacker-controlled hosts, an approach it calls token spraying. It counts more than 200,000 failed sign-ins from 193.26.115.0/24 (AS210558, 1337 Services GmbH), 497 successful Microsoft 365 sign-ins, 97 compromised accounts in 79 organizations and 48 rogue Entra devices. In at least 19 organizations the attacker removed existing MFA methods and registered its own authenticator within three hours of the first sign-in, then hid mail about payroll, deposits and bonuses with short-named inbox rules. The replayed sessions used Microsoft first-party clients (Microsoft Office, Microsoft Authentication Broker, OfficeHome) with node or bare Mozilla/5.0 user agents.

timeline.text: First activity in the campaign window Huntress measured.
In one case an authenticator named 'iPhone 13' was activated less than 51 minutes after the session was hijacked.
Last activity in the measured window.
Huntress publishes the analysis.
The Hacker News reports it.

stories.rootCause: Credentials and MFA were relayed through adversary-in-the-middle phishing pages, and the resulting tokens were replayed from hosting infrastructure; Conditional Access did not require MFA or block for every client app type, and device-code flow was not restricted.
attacker: Replayed stolen tokens from 193.26.115.0/24 and other 1337 Services addresses within minutes, across many organizations at once.
Used the Microsoft Office and Microsoft Authentication Broker clients with a node or bare Mozilla/5.0 user agent (Build A), and OfficeHome with a normal Chrome/Edge user agent (Build B).
Registered its own authenticator app after removing existing MFA methods in at least 19 organizations.
Joined 48 rogue devices to Entra ID, named DESKTOP- followed by eight hex characters.
Created inbox rules with names such as '.', 'sss', 'ss', 'iT', ',.', 's' and 'd' that deleted or moved payroll, deposit and bonus mail to RSS Feeds, RSS Subscriptions or Conversation History.
In one mailbox marked all mail read, deleted it and sent spam to hundreds of external recipients until Entra ID Protection flagged the user as high risk.
iocs: Rogue device names: DESKTOP-54521F46, DESKTOP-BAF88EF4, DESKTOP-CA85907C (pattern DESKTOP- + 8 hex)

apps.name: Microsoft Office
apps.did: Client application of the replayed sign-ins (Build A).
apps.action: Do not disable; hunt for its sign-ins from hosting IPs with a node or bare Mozilla/5.0 user agent

apps.name: Microsoft Authentication Broker
apps.did: Client application of replayed sign-ins (Build A), including Device Registration Service access used to join rogue devices.
apps.action: Do not disable; hunt for its sign-ins to Device Registration Service from hosting IPs

apps.name: OfficeHome
apps.did: Client application of replayed sign-ins (Build B) with a normal browser user agent.
apps.action: Do not disable; correlate with sign-ins from the listed ranges

stories.appsNote: Huntress names no attacker-created OAuth application; the IDs above are Microsoft's own clients the replay used. Resource IDs it lists (Microsoft Graph, Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Device Registration Service 01cb2876-7ebd-4aa4-9cc9-d28bd4d359a9) are the targets, not attacker apps.

remediation.text: Revoke the user's sessions and reset the password; a reset alone leaves attacker devices, MFA methods and a valid token in place.
Audit registered MFA methods for ones cleared and re-registered within minutes and remove any unrecognized authenticator.
Audit Entra devices named DESKTOP-, Device- or Work Pc plus eight hex characters, especially ones registered from hosting IPs; confirm before deleting.
Review inbox rules with punctuation-only or very short names, or that move mail to RSS or Conversation History folders or match payroll and banking terms.
Treat AADSTS53003 blocks as evidence of a valid stolen credential, not a successful defense.
Restrict device-code flow with a Conditional Access authentication-flows policy and require MFA or block for all users, all cloud apps and all client app types.

Hunt sign-in logs for the Microsoft Office or Authentication Broker client from AS210558 or 193.26.115.0/24 with a node or bare Mozilla/5.0 user agent, and alert on MFA method registration within three hours of a sign-in from a hosting ASN.
Block standard users from consenting to applications and review newly consented enterprise applications for the affected users.

stories.title: Fake IT support over Teams external chat: mail bombing, throwaway onmicrosoft.com tenants and RMM tools lead to GoGRPC, Python implants and Chaos ransomware
stories.summary: Arctic Wolf Labs (26 October 2026) describes a recurring pattern across hundreds of cases: the victim's inbox is flooded with subscription mail, then an 'IT support' account from a throwaway tenant (30-40% on onmicrosoft.com fallback domains) opens a Teams external chat and talks the user into a remote session through Quick Assist, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, TeamViewer or another RMM tool. Instead of pasting links, the attacker has the user run PowerShell that pulls an MSI from Azure Blob Storage, which unpacks a Python implant; a second MSI queries Active Directory over LDAP for every computer and user and sends the result out. Follow-on activity includes the GoGRPC backdoor, Level RMM for redundancy, lateral movement to domain controllers, exfiltration and ransomware; the activity aligns with STAC4749, linked by Sophos to Chaos ransomware.

timeline.text: Arctic Wolf Labs publishes the analysis with tenant domains and .top infrastructure.
The Hacker News reports it.

stories.rootCause: Teams external access open to any tenant (including trial tenants), users able to accept remote-control sessions from an unsolicited contact, and RMM tools that could be installed or run without approval.
attacker: Mail-bombed the target with newsletter and subscription confirmations.
Opened Teams external chats from throwaway tenants with IT-themed display names (Help Desk, IT Support, IT Service Desk - Liam, HelpDesk Supervisor).
Gained hands-on-keyboard access through Quick Assist, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, TeamViewer, Atera, Zoho Assist, NetSupport or LogMeIn.
Had the user run PowerShell that downloaded an MSI from Azure Blob Storage, dropping a Python implant (ss.py, cleaner.ps1 under AppData\Local\PowershellCleaner\scripts).
Enumerated all Active Directory users and computers over LDAP and exfiltrated the results; deployed GoGRPC and Level RMM; moved to domain controllers and deployed ransomware.

remediation.text: Switch Teams external access from allow-all to an allow-list of specific external domains.
Block federation with trial tenants: Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -ExternalAccessWithTrialTenants "Blocked".
Block chat with unmanaged Teams accounts and stop them from starting conversations with your users.
Enable 'Allow my security team to manage blocked domains' and add the listed tenant domains to the Defender Tenant Allow/Block List.
Restrict Quick Assist to authorized IT roles and block or uninstall unsanctioned RMM tools through Defender for Endpoint or application control.
Require out-of-band verification for every remote-access request and tell staff how real IT contacts them.

Search CloudAppEvents for ChatCreated with a participant from the listed onmicrosoft.com tenants and, on hits, look on that user's device for an RMM process start followed by PowerShell, msiexec and LDAP queries.

stories.title: YAM Store (Storm-3119) and the Storm-2990 phishing kits: a marketplace of hijacked Microsoft 365 tenants and phishing-as-a-service, disrupted by Microsoft DCU
stories.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Digital Crimes Unit (14 October 2026) describe YAM Store, a Chinese-language initial-access marketplace tracked as Storm-3119 that sells compromised or fraudulently created Microsoft and Google environments, credentials and infrastructure, and Storm-2990, the developers of the CoGUI, Haozi and Iron Man System phishing kits sold through it. Microsoft says the kits' operators facilitated over one billion phishing emails and SMS messages to more than 75,000 organizations since January 2026. YAM Store discovers Microsoft 365 tenants, takes them over with compromised client secrets in an app-only flow, and abuses a compromised Global Administrator to provision the PnP Management Shell service principal with broad Graph and SharePoint permissions for bulk hosting. Microsoft DCU, with law enforcement and partners, disrupted the ecosystem's primary developers and infrastructure.

timeline.text: From January 2026 the kits' operators facilitate over one billion phishing emails and SMS messages to more than 75,000 organizations (Microsoft's figure; start month only).
Iron Man System starts being advertised through YAM Store (Microsoft gives the month only).
Microsoft publishes the analysis; the Digital Crimes Unit facilitated disruption of the primary developers and infrastructure with law enforcement and partners.

stories.rootCause: Compromised client secrets of applications in victim tenants (used in an application-only authentication flow) and compromised Global Administrator accounts, plus fraudulently created tenants backed by fake organizations.
attacker: Discovered Microsoft 365 tenants and their licensing with automated Flask-based tooling run over Tor.
Used compromised client secrets in an app-only flow to reset passwords, assign education licences and grant privileged attributes silently.

Signed in as a compromised Global Administrator, provisioned the PnP Management Shell service principal and granted it broad Graph permissions (including AppCatalog.ReadWrite.All) and full SharePoint API control.
Abused SharePoint and OneDrive for bulk hosting and ran a custom DNS platform for phishing domains and certificates behind Cloudflare.
Sold phishing kits with geofencing, fake CAPTCHA gates, Telegram-bot exfiltration and WebSocket live victim interaction; downstream buyers ran credential phishing and device-code phishing.

Enable network protection.

stories.title: Masqueraded MSP360 RMM installer (v2.5.0.67) used to plant ConnectWise ScreenConnect through phishing lures
stories.summary: Microsoft Defender Experts observed phishing campaigns in July 2026, across multiple industries, that delivered a signed but masqueraded MSP360 RMM installer (v2.5.0.67) behind lures such as e-card and RSVP invitations, Zoom and Adobe Reader installers, document signing, job offers and delivery notices. Once a user ran it and approved UAC, the agent installed as two Windows services, opened UDP 48678 inbound and launched PowerShell that downloaded and silently installed ConnectWise ScreenConnect as a second remote-access channel. The actor then used ScreenConnect's RunFile feature to drop tools named to look like Windows, Defender or Phone Link components for credential theft, collection and hiding the session. Microsoft saw no exploitation of ScreenConnect itself and does not attribute the activity; it says the installer's signing certificate has since been revoked.

timeline.text: Defender Experts observe the phishing campaigns distributing the masqueraded MSP360 v2.5.0.67 installer; a separate July activity uses FaronicsDeployAgent.exe the same way (Microsoft gives the month only).

stories.rootCause: Users ran a signed remote-management installer delivered by phishing and approved its UAC prompt; legitimately obtained RMM software then gave the actor persistent, trusted remote access.
attacker: Hosted payloads on attacker domains, compromised sites, Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Dropbox, GitLab and Supabase.
Installed the MSP360 agent to C:\Program Files\RMM Agent\ as services RMM.Agent.exe and RMM.Agent.Launcher.exe, with Run keys and an inbound firewall rule on UDP 48678.

Block unapproved IT management tools with Application Control for Windows or AppLocker publisher rules, and use the Defender for Endpoint block-certificate action for signed installers.
Enable cloud-delivered protection and the ASR rules 'Use advanced protection against ransomware' and 'Block process creations originating from PsExec and WMI commands'.
Enforce MFA on the RMM platforms you approve.
Isolate a device that runs RMM.Agent.exe or a ScreenConnect client you did not deploy, uninstall both and remove the UDP 48678 firewall rule before reconnecting it.
Alert on new services or Run keys for remote-access tools outside your approved RMM list, and on processes started from \ScreenConnect\Temp\.

stories.title: Teams help-desk impersonation leading to AD CS abuse (ESC1 and ESC8), DCSync and Rclone exfiltration
stories.summary: Microsoft Security Research describes two intrusions, not attributed to a named actor, that began with Microsoft Teams messages and calls from organization-themed onmicrosoft.com tenants posing as IT support. Victims opened Quick Assist and shared the code, giving the attacker hands-on-keyboard access; staged Python, Bun or Java runtimes ran payloads from KB-prefixed folders under the user profile. In the first case an ESC1-vulnerable certificate template let the attacker obtain certificates for eleven privileged accounts, run DCSync within seconds and later exfiltrate file-server data with Rclone renamed SearchApp.exe through an account excluded from automated response. In the second case PetitPotam coercion was relayed to AD CS Web Enrollment (ESC8) to obtain a domain controller certificate used for PKINIT; Defender alerted and the workstation was isolated before further progress.

timeline.text: Microsoft Security Blog publishes the analysis of both cases; no intrusion dates are given beyond that. In case 1 a second Teams wave against 16 users followed about 90 minutes after the first session was disrupted.

stories.rootCause: Social engineering over Teams to obtain a Quick Assist session, then an ESC1 certificate template that accepts requester-supplied identity with broad enrollment rights (case 1) and an AD CS Web Enrollment endpoint accepting NTLM without relay protection (case 2). Issued certificates and Kerberos tickets survive password resets and reimaging.
attacker: Teams chats and calls from help-desk-themed external onmicrosoft.com tenants
Quick Assist remote control granted by the victim
Portable Python, Bun (renamed executable) and Java runtimes run from KB-prefixed folders under the user profile
Discovery with ipconfig /all and tasklist; LDAPS and SMB to domain infrastructure
ESC1 certificate requests for privileged accounts, then DCSync
PetitPotam (EFSRPC) coercion relayed to /certsrv for a Domain Controller certificate, then PKINIT
Rclone renamed SearchApp.exe copying file-server data to an external SFTP destination

Allow only approved remote-support tools and workflows; alert when Quick Assist or an RMM session extracts archives or launches scripts from user-writable paths.
Use App Control for Business to block unapproved portable runtimes (Bun, Python, Java) and script execution from user-writable locations.

Apply KB5005413 guidance against NTLM relay to AD CS: require HTTPS with Extended Protection for Authentication on enrollment endpoints, disable NTLM there where Kerberos works, and remove unneeded Web Enrollment and CES endpoints.

Review authentication-capable certificate templates for requester-supplied subject, broad enrollment rights and weak issuance controls; use Defender for Identity AD CS posture assessments to find ESC1 and ESC8 exposure.
Enable Certification Services advanced auditing (success and failure) with the CA audit filter, and preserve CA, IIS, endpoint, identity and Teams logs.
Revoke unauthorized certificates and publish revocation; handle already-issued Kerberos tickets separately because revocation does not invalidate them.
Treat exclusions from automated containment as incident decisions and assign manual compensating actions for every excluded identity or device.

Run the post's four advanced hunting queries (Teams external contact, Bun or Java from KB-prefixed paths, network activity of those runtimes, AD CS relay and PKINIT alerts with evidence) over the last 30 days and review Defender for Identity ESC1/ESC8 alerts.

List certificate templates with ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT and Client Authentication EKU that Domain Users or Authenticated Users can enroll, and remove the enrollment right or require manager approval this week.

stories.title: Tampered Claude Code-branded extension in the Cursor marketplace (2.1.312 and 2.1.313) installs a persistent SSH reverse-tunnel backdoor
stories.summary: A tampered copy of the anthropic.claude-code extension, versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, was served by the Cursor extension marketplace from about 2:27 AM to 1:35 PM PDT before Cursor reported it on 29 October 2026; Anthropic says it did not develop the package and the Visual Studio Marketplace and npm package were not affected. On load the extension collected host details, the Git email and up to forty environment-variable names, appended an Ed25519 key with the comment svc-telemetry to authorized_keys and opened an SSH reverse tunnel to 134.209.82[.]225, persisting through a LaunchAgent, an @reboot crontab entry or a SysMon scheduled task. timeline.text: Cursor reports the malicious extension versions; they were live from about 02:27 to 13:35 PDT.

stories.rootCause: A tampered copy of a popular AI-assistant extension was published to and served by the Cursor marketplace; developers installing or auto-updating received it. Microsoft does not state how the package got into the marketplace.
attacker: Reconnaissance of host, user, OS, Git email and secret-like environment-variable names
Ed25519 key with comment svc-telemetry appended to authorized_keys (including administrators_authorized_keys on Windows)
SSH reverse tunnel -N -R '*:0:localhost:22' with host-key checking off, via autossh or a hidden PowerShell loop
Persistence: ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist (macOS), @reboot crontab (Linux), SysMon scheduled task or sysmon.cmd in Startup (Windows)

remediation.text: Hunt for affected installs, preserve the extension package, modified SSH files, keys, scripts and startup configuration, and isolate devices showing loader execution or backdoor installation.

Remove the exact svc-telemetry key by fingerprint while keeping unrelated keys, stop the SSH tunnel processes, delete .stk_ files after collection, inspect and remove the persistence objects, and remove the extension.
Review telemetry for key acceptance, tunnel processes and command execution; rotate credentials and revoke sessions where exposure is indicated, rebuilding the device if needed.
Restrict editor extensions to approved publishers and set an extension installation cooldown, as Cursor advises.

Run the post's DeviceNetworkEvents, DeviceFileEvents and ScheduledTaskCreated queries over 30 days and treat any hit on a developer device as an incident: rotate the cloud and Git tokens that device's user held.

stories.title: Fake-download campaign: trojanized Inno Setup-style installers install WorldProxyPool proxyware, BOINC/CharityEngine and adware in one session
stories.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes an evolving fake-download campaign whose lures are cracked commercial software, free games, activators and unofficial utilities. The download is a trojanized Inno Setup-style installer that stages executables under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\ and calls rotating infrastructure with a d=inno and r=offer_execution pattern, installing several monetized 'offers' in one session. The payloads monetize the device through WorldProxyPool proxyware (SYSTEM-level scheduled tasks), CharityEngine and BOINC distributed computing, and AW Manager or Windows Manager adware-style utilities. Microsoft names no actor and does not state whether the campaign is still running; it describes the infrastructure as rotating frequently.

timeline.text: Microsoft Security Blog publishes the analysis with IOCs, Defender detections and three advanced hunting queries.

stories.rootCause: Users download software from untrusted sources (cracked software, key generators, unofficial game installers, activation tools); the installer itself is the delivery vehicle.
attacker: Lures: cracked software, free games, activators, unofficial utilities
Trojanized Inno Setup-style installer stages eld*.exe, set_*.exe, FirstFast[1].exe or SecondRunner[1].exe under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\
Callbacks carrying d=inno with r=offer_execution or r=offer_execution_fail to rotating .xyz and .cfd domains
WorldProxyPool proxyware (C:\Program Files\WorldProxyPool\sdk-agent.exe) persisted by SYSTEM scheduled tasks WorldProxyPoolAgent, WorldProxyPoolWatchdog, WorldProxyPoolUpdater
CharityEngine / BOINC distributed computing and AW Manager or Windows Manager adware-style utilities

remediation.text: Investigate execution from Inno temporary directories, especially staged eld*.exe, set_*.exe, FirstFast[1].exe or SecondRunner[1].exe files.
Correlate outbound requests containing d=inno with r=offer_execution or r=offer_execution_fail and review process, file and network activity across the whole installer session.

Review newly created scheduled tasks, particularly those running as SYSTEM or performing watchdog or updater functions, and audit software inventory for WorldProxyPool, CharityEngine, BOINC or VirtualBox.

Enable Defender Antivirus cloud-delivered protection, keep tamper protection on, enable SmartScreen reputation-based protection and evaluate ASR rules such as blocking executables that do not meet prevalence, age or trusted-list criteria.

Run the post's three advanced hunting queries (DeviceNetworkEvents and DeviceProcessEvents) over 30 days and isolate any device with a WorldProxyPool scheduled task: a proxyware exit node makes other people's traffic appear to come from your network.

stories.title: ARTEX agentic AI framework hunts leaked app secrets on GitHub and turns them into service principal sign-ins, Key Vault exfiltration and Azure AI abuse
stories.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence, which began seeing its GitHub secret searches in August 2026, describes an agentic AI offensive framework, ARTEX, that searches GitHub for leaked secrets tied to a target organization, cloud services or AI providers, then uses valid leaked application credentials to sign in as service principals to Entra ID tenants and connected Azure and Microsoft 365 resources. From there the agents harvest more credentials (storage keys, App Service settings, connection strings, publishing credentials, AKS credentials), read SharePoint, OneDrive and mailbox content, enumerate subscriptions and AI deployments, and exfiltrate Key Vault secrets. Failed Azure Resource Manager calls were corrected and retried within about a minute, and in one case the path from GitHub search to Key Vault exfiltration took five minutes. Microsoft names no Storm group and publishes no application IDs.

timeline.text: Earliest observed successful service principal sign-ins from 199.19.77[.]84 across multiple application IDs.
Microsoft Security Blog publishes the analysis with IOCs, detections and five advanced hunting queries.

stories.rootCause: Application secrets and API keys leaked in code repositories stayed valid; service principals holding them had broad Azure and Microsoft 365 reach and no Conditional Access for workload identities.
attacker: GitHub searches combining the target organization name with secret, cloud-service or AI-provider keywords
Service principal sign-ins with leaked app credentials, mainly from 199.19.77[.]84 and the Tor exit node 199.19.77[.]18
Calls returning storage account keys, App Service settings, connection strings, publishing credentials, AI/ML datastores and AKS user credentials
SharePoint and OneDrive downloads, mailbox-item access and Microsoft Graph searches for content of interest
Enumeration of subscriptions, resource groups, permissions, AI model deployments and service configurations
Adaptive retries: HTTP 400 ARM requests corrected by API version or method and retried roughly 28, 60 and 80 seconds later
Tokens for a single-tenant OAuth app used to exfiltrate Key Vault secrets, search Azure DevOps for secrets and run Azure Run Command on VMs
Validation and possible abuse of compromised Azure AI services
stories.appsNote: Microsoft names a multitenant application credential and a single-tenant OAuth application in the target organization but prints no application ID.

remediation.text: Block 199.19.77[.]84 as a named location in a Conditional Access policy for workload identities assigned to service principals, plus a user-scoped block policy; block the exact IP, not the whole ASN (workload identity policies need Workload ID Premium and cover single-tenant apps only).

For affected apps remove client secrets, certificates and federated credentials, including any the attacker added, and disable the service principal if needed; tokens already issued stay valid until they expire.
Revoke Entra sessions, Azure DevOps PATs and SSH keys for affected users.
Rotate every secret in any Key Vault the affected app could read, and credentials found in documents it accessed.
Review service principal and non-interactive sign-in logs for both IPs, failures included; AADSTS7000215 or AADSTS7000222 followed by a success is urgent.

Review Azure Activity, Key Vault and Storage diagnostics, Entra audit, Azure DevOps audit and the Microsoft 365 unified audit log; check PAT creation and first use, federated service connections and pipeline changes.
Alert when one IP authenticates to three or more service principals with mixed results, or one app requests tokens for ARM, Key Vault, Storage and Graph within a short window.

Enable Defender for Cloud plans for Resource Manager, Storage, Key Vault, App Service and Databases, apply least privilege to workload identities and move OAuth apps from secrets to managed identities.
Turn on GitHub secret scanning with push protection for every organization repository and list the app registrations whose secrets appear in any scan result; rotate them before investigating further.
Inventory app registrations that still use client secrets and have Key Vault, Storage or Azure AI data-plane roles; put them first in the managed-identity migration.

stories.title: Microsoft's Q3 2026 email threat report: 7.3 billion phishing threats, device-code QR lure against law firms and an Agent Tesla campaign with passing SPF/DKIM/DMARC
stories.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Defender Security Research Team counted about 7.3 billion email phishing threats from July to September 2026, nearly 3 billion of them in September (+41% on August). QR-code phishing fell 67% on Q2 while CAPTCHA-gated phishing nearly doubled from July to September, with SVG attachments carrying up to 65% of it. Two campaigns are described with indicators: a 19-20 August 'Salary Review' Word lure whose QR code led to a fake OneDrive page using device code phishing against over 10,000 users at 4,800 mostly US legal organizations, and a 21 September Spanish-language purchase-order and payroll campaign that delivered Agent Tesla to over 56,000 users at 8,100 organizations from a domain that passed SPF, DKIM and DMARC. In September tenant-level exception overrides applied to 63% of spoofed business-service messages with a recorded outcome, which Microsoft flags as a reason to review allow-lists.

Spanish-language purchase order and payroll campaign from contacto06@carloxmextos[.]org delivers Agent Tesla.

stories.rootCause: Phishing that rides trusted delivery paths: authenticated sender domains, spoofed business-service brands let through by broad tenant exception overrides, and device code flows that yield a session token without a password or a new MFA prompt.
attacker: Spoofed business-service sender domains (about 129 million messages in Q3; DocuSign 29% of September)
QR codes in PDF, DOC/DOCX and email bodies leading to credential pages
CAPTCHA-gated phishing pages, mostly via SVG attachments
Device code phishing behind a fake OneDrive sign-in page (August campaign)
Nested RAR archive with a JavaScript downloader fetching a PowerShell payload, and a double-extension executable, both leading to Agent Tesla (September campaign)
Teams call attempts with personal-name display names (about 141,000 in Q3)

Run the two EmailEvents queries for the campaign senders and review sign-ins of any recipient who clicked.
Review tenant- and user-level security exceptions; broad overrides let spoofed messages through.
Apply the recommended EOP and Defender for Office 365 settings, Safe Links and Safe Attachments, Defender for Endpoint network protection and SmartScreen-capable browsers.
Restrict external Teams access to who may chat or meet with outside parties and train users to verify external senders; run attack simulation training including Teams phishing.
Require phishing-resistant MFA for privileged accounts through Conditional Access and move users to passwordless sign-in where supported; keep automatic attack disruption on in Defender XDR.
Block the device code flow with a Conditional Access authentication-flows policy for everyone who has no documented need for it, since the August lure relied on it.

Alert on the Defender detections the report lists, among them 'Suspicious activity likely indicative of a connection to an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing site' and 'Email messages containing malicious URL removed after delivery'.

stories.title: AgtaBackup RAT: fake video-meeting installers enrol victims in signed RMM tools, then the attacker installs a .NET credential-stealing RAT
stories.summary: Unit 42 (Palo Alto Networks) documented the AgtaBackup RAT campaign on 28 September 2026, as reported by PCrisk on 16 October. A fake download page imitating a Microsoft Store listing for a video-conferencing app delivers a legitimately signed RMM installer (LogMeIn Resolve, ConnectWise ScreenConnect); once the victim accepts the UAC prompt the machine is enrolled in the attacker's RMM account. Hours or days later the attacker runs PowerShell through the RMM terminal to install the RAT, which steals browser credentials and cookies, logs keystrokes, takes screenshots and runs a hidden desktop. Detect FYI published a write-up on 8 November naming fake Google Meet updates as a lure; this routine could not open it (HTTP 403), so that detail is not confirmed here.

timeline.text: Unit 42 publishes its timely threat intel note on the AgtaBackup RAT campaign.
PCrisk describes the chain, the persistence tasks and the binary names.
Detect FYI publishes 'Fake Google Meet Updates, Abused RMM Tools, the AgtaBackup RAT Ecosystem & Campaign' (not readable by this routine).

stories.rootCause: A user installs a signed RMM agent from a fake meeting-app download page and accepts its UAC prompt, which hands the attacker remote administration of the device without any exploit.
attacker: Imitates a Microsoft Store listing for a video-conferencing app to deliver a signed RMM installer (LogMeIn Resolve, ConnectWise ScreenConnect).
Enrols the device in an attacker-controlled RMM account and later runs PowerShell through the RMM terminal to install the RAT.
Persists through two SYSTEM scheduled tasks, AgtaBackupAgentWatchdog and AgtaBackupAgentGuardian, that run every minute and reinstall the service within 60 seconds.
Hides its service from standard admin tools with a restrictive security descriptor; main binary 'Credential Guard.exe', helpers 'Dell Window Guard.exe' and 'Dell.Virus.Guard.exe'.
Steals browser credentials and cookies (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, Vivaldi, Firefox and others), logs keystrokes, takes screenshots and opens a hidden desktop session (AgtaBackstage).
Bypasses UAC by disabling the secure desktop in the registry and injecting keystrokes through a named pipe.

remediation.text: Isolate any device where the AgtaBackupAgentWatchdog or AgtaBackupAgentGuardian task exists and remove the RMM agent the attacker enrolled; the tasks reinstall the service within 60 seconds, so delete the tasks before the service.

Revoke sessions and reset passwords for every user who signed in through a browser on an affected device, because the RAT harvests browser credentials and cookies; in Entra, use Revoke sessions on the user and review their sign-ins for token replay.
Hunt Defender for Endpoint for the two scheduled task names and the three binary names, and for RMM agents (ScreenConnect, LogMeIn Resolve) installed outside your own RMM tenant.

Block or allow-list RMM software with Defender for Endpoint indicators or App Control so only the RMM product your organisation runs can install, and tell users meeting apps never require an update from a web page.
Alert on scheduled task creation with the AgtaBackup names (query below).

stories.title: GSocket (gs-netcat) as C2 on compromised Linux web servers: relay traffic through the Global Socket Relay Network leaves no attacker IP to block
stories.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence published on 11 November 2026 that multiple unrelated threat actors use the open-source GSocket client (gs-netcat) as command and control on Linux servers. Attackers gain remote code execution through an internet-facing web application (PHP and cPanel hosting, Apache, Java and Node web apps), fetch a script with curl, stage the client in /dev/shm and disguise it with kernel-thread-like names. Persistence is layered across cron, systemd units, shell profiles and watchdogs. Both the host and the operator connect outbound to the public Global Socket Relay Network, so there is no attacker-owned IP or domain to block. Defender for Endpoint detections rose 356.2% over the March 2026 baseline across March to August 2026; in a few incidents attackers tried CVE-2026-43284 (Dirty Frag) for root.

timeline.text: Start of the Defender for Endpoint telemetry period Microsoft analysed (March to August 2026); GSocket detections later rose 356.2% over the March baseline.
Microsoft Security Blog publishes the analysis, IOCs, detection names and advanced hunting queries.

stories.rootCause: An unpatched internet-facing web application allows remote code execution, and unrestricted outbound traffic lets the installed GSocket client reach the public relay network.
attacker: Exploits an internet-facing web application for remote code execution and runs a remote script fetched with curl.
Profiles the host, picks the GSocket client for its architecture (x86-64 or AArch64) and stages it under /dev/shm/.gs-0/.
Masquerades the process with kernel-thread-like names such as [kaluad] and removes staging files.
Persists through cron, systemd units with service-like names (systemd-remount-d, defunct.service), shell profiles and watchdogs.
Delivers the shared secret by stdout, a temporary file, Telegram (GS_TG_TOKEN, GS_TG_CHATID), Discord or a webhook.
In a few incidents attempts CVE-2026-43284 (Dirty Frag) to escalate from the web-service account to root.

remediation.text: On an affected host remove the GSocket client, its persistence (cron entries, systemd units, shell profile lines, watchdogs) and staged files, then verify outbound relay connections have stopped.
Patch and harden internet-facing web applications, CMS platforms, plugins and application servers; remove unused components and restrict upload and admin paths.
Apply deny-by-default egress on internet-facing servers, allow only required destinations and monitor relay connections.
Mount temporary and memory-backed directories as non-executable where feasible and alert on execution from hidden or world-writable paths.
Prioritise local privilege-escalation patches (CVE-2026-43284) on internet-facing Linux servers.
Enable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Linux with real-time and cloud-delivered protection and behaviour monitoring of web-service child processes.

Run Microsoft's published advanced hunting queries for GSocket process activity, installer downloads and the staging paths across every onboarded Linux server for the last 30 days, and isolate any match before removing the client.

Add a custom detection on DeviceProcessEvents for command lines containing gsocket.io, gs-netcat or GS_TG_TOKEN on Linux devices, so a new installation raises an incident rather than waiting for a hunt.

kql.title: Processes running from the GSocket staging path (Defender XDR advanced hunting)
kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath startswith "/dev/shm/.gs-" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gs-netcat", "gsocket.io", "GS_TG_TOKEN")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

stories.title: Microsoft 365 outage lures: high-volume phishing claims held mail will be deleted in 24 hours and links to reallifeaccounting[.]com
stories.summary: On 13 November 2026 Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign against organisations in many sectors. The emails pose as Microsoft 365 service-health notices (subject 'Outage - <6 random characters>', display names such as 'MSF Outage Notification' or 'AMZ Service Health') and claim that messages held during an Exchange Online outage will be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient selects RESTORE MESSAGES. Recipient-specific tracking links lead to reallifeaccounting[.]com. Microsoft assesses it as likely credential phishing but saw no credential capture, malware or post-compromise activity and has not attributed it to a named actor. Defender for Office 365 blocks and quarantines the messages.

timeline.text: Date of the fictitious Exchange Online incident the lure body refers to.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence observes the campaign: sender domains moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, newbooker[.]com; clicks lead to reallifeaccounting[.]com.

stories.rootCause: Users trust messages that look like Microsoft 365 service-health notices; the lure uses urgency (deletion in 24 hours), randomized subjects and recipient-specific tracking links on shared email-delivery infrastructure to avoid simple pattern matching.
attacker: Sends from a cluster of sender domains (moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, newbooker[.]com) with display names built from a three-character organisation-style prefix plus 'Outage Notification' or 'Service Health'.
Uses subjects 'Outage - <random token>' and hides a fake email conversation in the body, which Microsoft reads as an attempt at mail-filter evasion.
Routes the RESTORE MESSAGES or TAKE ACTION click through recipient-specific tracking URLs to reallifeaccounting[.]com (path /themelist0.html in some samples).

remediation.text: Search mail telemetry for the sender domains, the 'Outage -' subject pattern, the display names and the destination domain; quarantine matches and remove delivered copies.
Block or closely monitor reallifeaccounting[.]com and /themelist0.html; do not block the shared email-delivery infrastructure on this campaign alone.
Identify users who selected the links from click telemetry, proxy logs and endpoint evidence, and whether the destination was reached.

For any user who may have entered credentials: reset the password, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, verify MFA registrations, and review sign-ins, OAuth consent, inbox and forwarding rules, delegates and unusual Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive or Teams access.

Require phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys or security keys), enable Safe Links, Safe Attachments and Zero-hour auto purge, and train users that service-health notices never send them to a non-Microsoft domain to recover mail.
Add a mail-flow or custom detection rule that flags inbound messages whose display name contains 'Outage Notification' or 'Service Health' from a sender domain that is not microsoft.com or your own.

stories.title: Optimizely Web Experimentation supply-chain attack: malicious Project JavaScript served from cdn.optimizely.com to 178 organisations
stories.summary: On 16 November 2026 an attacker exploited a vulnerability in the account signup flow of Optimizely Web Experimentation and inserted malicious code into the Project JavaScript field of customer projects, so Optimizely's own CDN served it to visitors of the customers' sites. Report URI identified 188 infected snippets tied to 178 organisations, among them the BBC, CNN, Zoom, GitLab, IKEA and HSBC. The sample Socket analysed is a wallet clipper that swaps cryptocurrency addresses in page text and the clipboard, plus a loader that fetches a second script for iOS devices; later versions are reported to skim payment cards. Optimizely says it patched the flaw, removed the code, revoked tokens and reset access for affected accounts. The affected sites themselves were not compromised; the risk sits with their visitors and with any page where such a script runs next to credentials or payment fields.

timeline.text: The attacker exploits the Optimizely Web Experimentation signup-flow vulnerability; the first malicious build in the published timeline is at 08:10 UTC (StepSecurity, cited by Socket).

Socket publishes its static analysis of a track.js sample and the indicators below.

stories.rootCause: A vulnerability in the Optimizely Web Experimentation account signup flow let the attacker write to the Project JavaScript field of customer projects, which Optimizely's CDN then served on every page carrying the snippet (Optimizely's statement as reported by Socket).
attacker: Inserted obfuscated JavaScript into the Project JavaScript field of customer projects
Ran a wallet clipper that replaces cryptocurrency addresses in page text, inputs and the clipboard
Loaded a second-stage boot.js for devices classified as iOS

remediation.text: Check whether your sites load an Optimizely Web Experimentation snippet and review the Project JavaScript of every project for code you did not write.
Search proxy, DNS and endpoint network logs for 1688360[.]cc and 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu from 16 November 2026 onwards.
Reconsider whether experimentation and personalisation scripts need to run across the whole site, particularly on payment, account and other sensitive pages.
Rotate the Optimizely account credentials and API tokens your organisation uses and review who can edit project code.

stories.title: Microsoft Entra Connect Health API flaw: attackers read administrator emails and tenant metadata (23 Jul - 19 Nov 2026)
stories.summary: A vulnerability in the Microsoft Entra Connect Health API, introduced on 23 July 2026 and detected by Microsoft on 9 November, let unauthorized callers read tenant-level metadata. Microsoft fixed it in the cloud service on 19 November and concluded on 20 November that attackers had read tenant data; customers have nothing to patch. The records included administrator and technical-contact email addresses, tenant ID, display name, initial domain, country, Entra license tier, directory-sync state and Connect Health onboarding. Microsoft says passwords, hashes, sign-in tokens, valid keys, Azure subscription details and on-premises AD topology were not exposed and it found no changes to monitoring settings. It has not said who exploited the flaw or how many tenants were affected; the main risk for an affected tenant is targeted phishing of its administrators.

timeline.text: Vulnerability introduced into the Entra Connect Health API.
Microsoft detects the vulnerability.
Microsoft deploys a fix in the cloud service; no customer patch.
Investigation concludes that attackers read tenant data; Microsoft notifies affected customers (notice shared on Reddit).

stories.rootCause: A flaw in Microsoft's cloud-side Entra Connect Health API returned tenant-level contact and configuration metadata to unauthorized callers for about 109 days before detection.
attacker: Unknown actor (Microsoft has not attributed it) read tenant metadata through the Entra Connect Health API, including administrator and technical-contact email addresses.

remediation.text: Check the security advisory in Azure Service Health in the Azure portal to see whether your tenant is listed.
Run Microsoft's read-only GetTenant PowerShell script (aka.ms/ConnectHealth/scripts) to see which metadata of your tenant was exposed.
Alert IT and security teams to targeted phishing of administrators and confirm the tenant's technical-contact details.
Require phishing-resistant MFA for privileged accounts and use Privileged Identity Management where available.
Review Connect Health settings, Entra audit and sign-in logs and Azure Activity Logs.
Run the three queries below for the exposed admin and technical-contact addresses: phishing and first-contact mail, flagged or clicked-through links, risky or new-country sign-ins since 9 Nov 2026.

stories.title: M365 token spray and replay campaign: AiTM and device-code tokens replayed from 193.26.115.0/24 against 79 organisations
stories.summary: Between 14 July and 22 September 2026 Huntress tracked a Microsoft 365 campaign that captured post-MFA session tokens through adversary-in-the-middle relays and device-code phishing and replayed them from the 193.26.115.0/24 block of 1337 Services GmbH (AS210558). Huntress responded at 79 organisations, with at least 497 successful sign-ins against more than 200,000 failed attempts. After access the attacker registered fake Entra-joined devices named DESKTOP- plus eight hex characters, wiped and replaced MFA methods, and created hidden inbox rules with one-to-three-character names that moved mail to RSS or Conversation History folders. In one case the rules were used for payroll fraud against an external accountant. Huntress published the report on 22 October 2026; no activity after 22 September is reported.

timeline.text: First detection: sign-in from 193.26.115[.]221 from an Entra-joined device named DESKTOP- plus eight hex characters.
AiTM relay 185.238.2[.]195 captures a victim at the MFA prompt at 17:18 UTC; the session is replayed from 193.26.115[.]199 at 17:30 and a new authenticator labelled iPhone 13 is activated at 18:08.
Phase 2 resumes from 193.26.115[.]16 and 193.26.115[.]21, including device-code phishing.
Phase 3 burst from 193.26.115[.]72; Huntress notifies 22 customers within two hours.
Final takeover: relay capture at 20:46, replay from 193.26.115[.]210 at 20:50.
Huntress publishes the campaign report.

stories.rootCause: Users completed MFA through attacker relays or entered device codes for the attacker, so the attacker held valid post-MFA tokens; a password reset alone did not end access because devices, MFA methods and live tokens stayed in place (Huntress).
attacker: Captured sessions with AiTM relays and device-code phishing
Replayed tokens with scripts (Build A, user agent node, OAuth2:Token) and browser sessions (Build B, Login:reprocess)
Registered at least 48 fake Entra-joined devices named DESKTOP- plus eight uppercase hex characters
Wiped existing MFA methods and registered their own authenticator
Created hidden inbox rules with short or punctuation-only names moving mail to RSS Feeds, RSS Subscriptions or Conversation History
Sent outbound spam and payroll-fraud email from compromised mailboxes

stories.appsNote: Target resources named by Huntress: Microsoft Graph, Office 365 Exchange Online, SharePoint Online and the Device Registration Service (01cb2876-7ebd-4aa4-9cc9-d28bd4d359a9).

remediation.text: Revoke sessions and reset passwords together; a reset alone leaves attacker devices, MFA methods and live tokens in place.
Audit Entra devices named DESKTOP- plus eight hex characters, especially those registered from hosting IPs; confirm before deleting, the pattern is not unique to this campaign.
Audit MFA methods cleared and re-registered within minutes and remove unrecognised authenticators.
Review inbox rules with short or punctuation-only names, rules moving mail to RSS or Conversation History folders, and rules keyed on payroll or banking terms.
Treat AADSTS53003 blocks as proof of a valid credential and reset it.
Restrict device-code flow with a Conditional Access authentication-flows policy and restrict user consent to applications.

Add 193.26.115.0/24 and the relay addresses to a Conditional Access named location blocked for sign-in, and require a compliant or hybrid-joined device for Exchange Online and the Device Registration Service.
Create a Sentinel analytics rule on new device registrations followed within three hours by an authentication-method change for the same user.
