stories.title: Azure API Management Classic: secrets stored in APIM read through a management-plane flaw (fixed 19 Nov 2026)
stories.summary: A flaw in the Classic tiers of Azure API Management (Developer, Basic, Standard, Premium) let an unauthorized party reach management functions of instances that were not configured to Microsoft's recommended practices, and with them the secrets stored in APIM: named values, client secrets of identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys and tokens for the direct management API. Microsoft identified the issue on 18 November and closed the access path on 19 November; the fix needs no customer action but does not invalidate credentials taken before it. Norway's NSM links the exploitation to attacks on Norwegian energy companies (Equinor, Skagerak Energi). Microsoft's advisory went to affected customers through Azure Service Health and is not public; the access path left no logs in the customer's tenant, so hunting looks at what the stolen secrets could open.

timeline.text: Microsoft identifies the security issue.
Microsoft closes the unauthorized access path and rotates Microsoft-controlled keys where appropriate.
Anders Kristiansen publishes what to check and six hunting steps with KQL.
BleepingComputer reports Microsoft's advisory and NSM's link to attacks on energy companies.
NSM: an unknown actor actively looked for access tokens, secrets and named values in APIM.

stories.rootCause: A management-plane access path in APIM Classic (a deprecated legacy endpoint, per the researchers' reading) that did not enforce authentication for instances outside Microsoft's recommended configuration - for example with the direct management API enabled or secrets stored in APIM instead of referenced from Key Vault.
attacker: Looked for access tokens, secrets and named values in APIM instances (NSM).
Could use the secrets to reach the applications, services and back-end systems they unlock, depending on each credential's permissions.

remediation.text: Rotate every secret stored in or used by APIM Classic: named values, identity-provider and OpenID Connect client secrets (in the app registrations), subscription keys, tenant access keys and the back-end credentials APIM sends.
Set 'Enable Management REST API' to No on every instance (the direct management API bypasses Entra ID and Azure RBAC and is retired).
Move secrets from APIM named values into Key Vault references, so APIM keeps a reference and the vault keeps the audit trail.
Inventory the app registrations whose client secrets were stored in APIM; after rotation, alert on any sign-in that still uses an old credential key (our query 3).
Check the Azure Service Health security advisory in the Azure portal for whether your subscriptions were notified.

| where type =~ "microsoft.apimanagement/service"
| extend tier = tostring(sku.name)
| where tier in~ ("Developer", "Basic", "Standard", "Premium")

stories.title: Fake Microsoft Teams meeting scheduler hides device code phishing behind a "Booking Reference"
stories.summary: Huntress describes a device code phishing attack it contained in mid-October 2026 against a construction company. A spear-phishing email from a typosquatted domain, registered eight days earlier, impersonated a senior vice president at another construction firm; the link passed through Microsoft Safe Links and a Google short link to a fake "Microsoft Teams Meeting Scheduler". After the victim picked a meeting slot, the backend started a real Microsoft device code sign-in and showed the user_code as a "Booking Reference", copied it to the clipboard and opened Microsoft's genuine device login page. The victim's paste completed authentication and the attacker obtained tokens through Microsoft Authentication Broker, routed through a residential proxy. The kit was AES-256-GCM encrypted in the browser and restarted the device code session when Microsoft asked for MFA.

timeline.text: Huntress SOC observes and contains the attack (the article says mid-October only; the 15th is a placeholder).
Huntress publishes the analysis with IOCs; no KQL is published.

stories.rootCause: The device code flow let a sign-in started by the attacker be completed by the victim on a legitimate Microsoft page. Huntress notes the compromised account had no MFA enrolled and was used from a non-compliant, unmanaged device; nothing blocked the device code flow.
attacker: Spear-phishing email impersonating a senior vice president from a typosquatted domain registered eight days before the attack.
Link wrapped in Safe Links, then redirected through a Google short link to evade URL reputation checks.
Fake Teams meeting scheduler that starts a Microsoft device code sign-in and displays the user_code as a Booking Reference.
Kit stored as AES-256-GCM ciphertext and decrypted in the browser; a fake "WinHello" verification pop-up; device code session restarted on AADSTS50076 or interaction_required.
Tokens received by Microsoft Authentication Broker (Cmsi:Cmsi login) through a residential callback proxy in New Orleans; python-requests and node user agents in sign-in logs.
iocs: User agents in sign-in logs: python-requests, node

remediation.text: Restrict device code authentication with a Conditional Access authentication-flows policy wherever it is not required, and monitor where it is.
Enforce phishing-resistant MFA and add Conditional Access policies for unmanaged and non-compliant devices.
After a confirmed compromise check for rogue MFA methods, unrecognised registered devices, unauthorised app consents, suspicious inbox rules and outbound mail.
Train users to verify booking or meeting requests through a known contact before entering any code on a Microsoft sign-in page.
For any user with a device code sign-in from python-requests or node, revoke sessions (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession) and reset credentials before investigating.
Block gpimmlgration[.]com and the share.google redirect in Defender for Endpoint indicators and Defender for Office 365 Tenant Allow/Block List.
Create a Sentinel analytics rule from the device code query below, alerting on device code sign-ins outside an approved device list.

kql.title: Device code sign-ins with programmatic user agents (Microsoft Sentinel)
kql.query:
// Teams booking flow device code phishing - device code sign-ins completed from scripts
// Microsoft Sentinel; diagnostic categories SignInLogs and NonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
union isfuzzy=true
  (SigninLogs | extend Kind = "interactive"),
  (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | extend Kind = "non-interactive")
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProtocol =~ "deviceCode" or OriginalTransferMethod =~ "deviceCodeFlow"
| extend UA = tolower(UserAgent)
| extend Scripted = UA has_any ("python-requests", "node")
| summarize SignIns = count(), Scripted = countif(Scripted), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10), UAs = make_set(UserAgent, 10), First = min(TimeGenerated), Last = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, Kind
| order by Scripted desc, SignIns desc
